courseDescriptionInputs.name: Psycholinguistics
courseDescriptionInputs.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

readerValues.programmeDescription: Study Italian language, literature and culture through language practice, linguistic analysis, literary history, film and cultural-political history, with supervised research and approved open study.
readerValues.comparisonExplanation: This qualified comparison relates the documented Italian Studies curriculum to a broader UCR program in literary interpretation, language analysis and cultural inquiry, including Renaissance Italy. UCR offers substantial close reading, stylistics, adaptation and historical/visual research. It does not reproduce advanced Italian proficiency, the Italian literary canon, dialectology or the full regional curriculum. A complete Leiden degree pathway is not certified.

cellNotes.text: Both develop analysis of poems and narrative texts. UCR supplies sustained close-reading methods; the chronological Italian movements and authors remain distinct.

Both include language processing, acquisition and neurolinguistic questions. UCR concentrates on experimental/neurocognitive inquiry; the complete phonetics, phonology and structural linguistics survey remains broader at Leiden.

Comparative literary reading, genres, framed storytelling and historical contexts provide a direct formal relationship. The specific medieval French/Italian traditions and manuscript corpus are not reproduced.
Both examine literary transmission, intertextuality and cultural exchange. UCR focuses on comparative myth and Ovidian retelling; Leiden specifically studies Italian-English circulation.
Both analyze cinematic/literary narrative, film form and historical movement contexts. The dedicated Italian Neorealism corpus, theory and case studies remain distinct.
Both study literary transposition across media and the consequences of adaptation. UCR develops text-film interpretation; Italian-Dutch interlingual translation practice is not supplied.

Renaissance Italy and its Mediterranean/global artistic connections address an identifiable part of Italian cultural history and transnational exchange. Leiden covers the broader medieval/early-modern political and cultural history; the art course is not a full substitute.
Data preparation, textual/web data, analysis and visualization supply a specific part of digital-humanities practice. The wider platform, interface and AI-theory curriculum remains different.
